corrected_value.authors: Yang, J., Wang, S., Xu, Y., & Rayner, K.
corrected_value.title: Do chinese readers obtain preview benefit from word n+2? Evidence from eye movements.

decisions.location: Experiment 1, Discussion, page 18, lines 439-446; References, page 44, lines 1089-1091
decisions.quote:
Experiment 1 was an attempt to replicate Yang et al.’s findings, and the analyses on
the regions examined by Yang et al. (i.e., words n, n+1, and n+2) provided a full replication.
Consistent with their findings, we observed n+2 preview effects of 22ms on word n+2 in gaze
duration when word n+1 was high-frequency. Yang et al. (2009) found a marginal (p=0.051)
effect in gaze duration of 22ms, and no effect in other measures. Furthermore, Yang et al.
(2012) did not find any effect of the word n+2 preview when a low-frequency word n+1 was
used. Thus, the pattern of effects was replicated in the current experiment, and our results are
consistent with Yang et al.’s findings.
decisions.reason: Experiment 1 explicitly re-tests the positive word n+2 preview benefit reported in Experiment 2 of Yang, Wang, Xu, and Rayner (2009) (doi:10.1037/a0013554) using its 20 high-frequency word n+1 stimuli, analysed as an independent subset alongside the 20 low-frequency word n+1 stimuli from Yang, Rayner, Li, and Wang (2012) (shipped row input_row_index 1497, doi:10.1007/s11145-010-9282-7). Shipped row 1497 represents only the 2012 low-frequency follow-up study; Yang et al. (2009) is a separate original publication with different authors, stimuli, experimental condition, and empirical finding, so report equivalence does not apply.
